qt: to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE), André Rougé (PfE), Marie-Luce Brasier-Clain (PfE), Valérie Deloge (PfE), Séverine Werbrouck (PfE), Pierre Pimpie (PfE) Subject:

While major fires have been breaking out across France and Europe, the existing Canadair fleets are ageing and no longer fit for purpose. On top of that, the Canadairs that have been ordered won’t be arriving anytime soon – the earliest batch will be arriving in 2028 and the later orders in 2032. Further to these new acquisitions, French and European companies (Positive Aviation, Kepplair Evolution, Hynaero, etc.) are working on innovative water bomber aircraft1, converting, for example, used ATR 72 aircraft into amphibious FF72 capable of scooping up 8 000 litres of water at half the cost. These projects would also reduce operating costs by 40 %. The idea of creating water-bombing drones is also being looked at, including by converting existing and decommissioned aircraft into drones. 1.
Is the Commission financing or is it prepared to finance the purchase of these new water-bombing planes or drones?
At the same time, would it be possible to obtain a licence to build Canadair in Europe?
https://x.com/AlexXplore/status/2080954114326876556?s=20. This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE).
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.11.2026) Since 2019, the EU is developing the future permanent rescEU fleet, financing the acquisition of 12 new firefighting airplanes and five helicopters. While the technical specifications of assets remain under the responsibility of Member States, the Commission is working with them and the industry to identify and closely monitor the development of potential new suitable European projects. These projects, if successful, could help strengthen Europe’s strategic and industrial autonomy and diversify the supply of aerial firefighting capabilities. However, developing new aircraft entails technical, safety and industrial challenges, with operational availability expected only in several years’ time. Modifying aircraft requests a bit less time but brings other challenges. Any EU support for the acquisition of such aircraft, including water-bombing drones, would need to be assessed under the applicable funding instruments and their eligibility requirements, taking account of operational needs, technical maturity, safety, costeffectiveness, and delivery schedules. The potential of unmanned aircraft for firefighting would also need to be assessed in light of their ability to operate safely and effectively alongside other firefighting aircraft and ground teams. Production of Canadair aircraft in Europe under licence would require an agreement with the holder of the relevant intellectual property rights, De Havilland Canada. So far, the manufacturer will keep his production line in Canada.
